narrative.text: Acknowledges the WHO departments, Guideline Development Group, Technical Working Group and chair involved in the home-based records guideline, and notes JICA funding without influence on content.
A list of acronyms and abbreviations used in the home-based records guideline.

Summarises the WHO guideline on home-based records, defining them as household-kept paper or electronic health documents ranging from vaccination cards to integrated maternal and child health books, whose benefits had not been systematically reviewed. It outlines development under the WHO handbook process with GRADE and an evidence-to-decision framework, and presents two recommendations: using home-based records to complement facility records, and that evidence is insufficient to favour any particular type or design. It also lists remarks on low-certainty evidence, privacy of HIV information, sustainable financing and further research needs.

Gives an overview of home-based records, describing their purpose in recording maternal, newborn and child health care and the different types in use, from maternal records and vaccination cards to integrated MCH books. It discusses their functions and global use and introduces the rationale and scope of the guideline. It ends by explaining how the priority questions and proximal and distal outcomes were chosen.

Describes how the guideline was developed according to the WHO handbook, including the roles of the WHO Steering Group, the 12-member Guideline Development Group, the Technical Working Group and external partners. It covers declarations of interest and the December 2016 scoping meeting that set six priority questions and outcomes. It explains evidence retrieval through systematic reviews, a qualitative evidence synthesis and a framework analysis of grey literature and key informant interviews, with certainty grading. It closes with the categories used for recommendations and the process of document preparation and peer review.

Presents the two recommendations on home-based records, with the rationale that although evidence certainty was low and studies were few, old and varied, benefits outweighed harms given positive effects on several care-seeking, home care and communication outcomes and use in at least 163 countries. It reviews the quantitative and qualitative evidence for each priority question, including values, acceptability, equity, resources and feasibility. Remarks address design, privacy and sustainable financing. The section ends with the evidence-to-decision framework table rating effects, certainty, costs, equity, acceptability and feasibility.

Sets out implementation considerations for home-based records, stressing planning and funding at every stage, government ownership, stakeholder involvement and harmonised content across health areas. It advises local adaptation and testing, design for low literacy, regular redesigns and attention to privacy. It also notes concerns about advertising on records and points to the Framework of Engagement with Non-State Actors for weighing risks.

Lists research gaps on home-based records, including the need for more and better-quality studies on health outcomes, standardised outcome measures and a logic model. It calls for research on effects on providers, comparisons of formats and electronic records, and cost-effectiveness of integrated records. It also identifies implementation questions such as design, durability, free versus paid distribution and incentive schemes.

Describes a meeting after the November 2017 consensus meeting to plan dissemination, which identified priorities such as a global coordinating platform, monitoring, training materials and harmonised research.

States that the guideline is expected to be updated in 2023 unless important new evidence emerges, with the Steering Group monitoring research and running a new scoping review near the end of that period.
The reference list for the home-based records guideline, citing mainly trials, Cochrane reviews, surveys and qualitative studies on parent-held and maternal and child health records.

Annex 1, listing the six priority guideline questions in PICO format and their main outcomes for maternal, newborn and child care-seeking, care practices, communication, morbidity and mortality, and health service outcomes.
Annex 2, listing WHO Steering Group members, regional office representatives, Guideline Development Group members, the technical team and external partner observers involved in the guideline.

Annex 3, describing how declarations of interest were collected and assessed through forms, CVs and online searches, with a table of each expert's declared interests and how any conflicts were managed.

Annex 4, tabulating studies that reported knowledge outcomes of home-based records, such as trials in Norway and Indonesia showing little or unclear difference in knowledge and studies of women's views on carrying their own notes.

Annex 5, detailing the evidence on effects of home-based records for each priority question, beginning with maternal care-seeking, care practices and morbidity in cluster trials of maternal and child health handbooks in Mongolia and Indonesia. It continues with newborn and child outcomes and with health service outcomes such as satisfaction and women's sense of control when holding their own notes, drawing on trials in the United Kingdom and Australia. Most effects are small or non-significant, with a few positive findings such as tetanus immunization, and certainty ranges from very low to moderate. The block ends with a list of names used for such records in different countries and WHO contact details.

The front matter of WHO recommendations on home-based records for maternal, newborn and child health (2018), with the copyright and ISBN page, licence terms, citation and table of contents including annexes and web annexes.
